You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: an instance you solve costs 1 for each wrong submission and 1 for
each demo request. An instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt
cap is reached, and one that ends unsolved costs the whole budget, 16, however
many submissions and demo requests it used. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

entry = rlm.harness.create_memory(title='ARC task-51335a5e: frames rise, open crosses sink (test unresolved)', id='arc_task_51335a5e_frames_rise_crosses_sink_unresolved', path='arc-patterns', global_=True, content='''For task-51335a5e, three demos show same-size input/output grids. Monochrome hollow rectangular frames (all four borders, enclosed zero interior) move upward to the top; open cross/plus-like objects move downward to the bottom. Keep object colors, shapes, and horizontal columns unchanged. Objects in the same class whose column spans overlap stack vertically while preserving their original top-to-bottom order; demonstrated by a 3x3 and 3x4 frame stacked at output rows 0-2 / 3-5, and overlapping cross objects stacked at rows 10-12 / 13-15. Objects of opposite classes can pass each other: demo3 has an upper open 8-cross and lower 8-frame in the same columns; output puts frame at top and cross at bottom. Non-overlapping objects align flush to their respective edges.\n\nImportant caveat: this simple rule repeatedly failed on the held-out test, so do not assume it is sufficient. Held-out input 16x15 contains a 3x3 color-3 frame at rows2-4 cols3-5; a 3x4 color-1 frame at rows6-8 cols4-7; a 5x5 color-1 frame at rows6-10 cols10-14; plus-like components color8 at rows3-6 cols0-2, color2 at rows1-4 cols10-14, and color2 at rows10-12 cols0-2. The color8 object physically touches the color3 frame at row4 (adjacent different-color components). All attempts were rejected, including: (1) separate-color components, frames top and open objects bottom, preserving original within-class order and stacking overlapping components; (2) reversing ring order; (3) reversing cross order; (4) both reverse orders (one attempt had an accidental malformed placement); (5-6) treating touching 8+3 as one component moved up, with different stacking; (7) treating 8+3 as one component moved down; (8) leaving touching composite in place while moving other objects. Thus the demonstrations establish only the basic directional pattern; test has a missing interaction/order nuance, possibly caused by the touching unlike-color objects or a more specific object-discovery/packing rule. Future recurrence: inspect exact segmentation/stacking carefully, don't repeat the naive frame-up/cross-down answer.' '')
print(entry)
